text:
Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls Review
Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls reviewed by Mitchell Saltzman on PC, also available on PlayStation 5.

In a genre where so many games end up missing a few key ingredients, Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls arrives as the total package. Its visuals are among ArcSystem Works’ best – and given the gorgeous ArcSys catalogue, that’s saying a whole lot. It breaks down one of a tag fighter’s most imposing barriers for new players by making it possible to be competitive with just one character. Its training tools are among the best I’ve seen, and even its story mode is great. The list just keeps going. The action can occasionally become hard to follow with all of the chaos happening on screen, but considering everything that Tokon nails, it’s hard to label the entire package as anything short of amazing.

text:
End of Oak Street Review
The End of Oak Street marks the return of David Robert Mitchell whose eerie It Follows has become a cult classic, but this time he's bringing JJ Abrams and a neighborhood full of dinosaurs! It's a surprisingly simple premise, a family mysteriously teleports to a swampy land of dinos and has to survive the ordeal with no idea how to get back home. While the writer/director wears the Spielberg influences of '80s and '90s family-focused adventure films proudly, do these creatures have the bite to live up to the films that inspired them?

Clint Gage reviews The End of Oak Street to talk about that, plus Anne Hathaway's incredible hot streak and why a split diopter lens is an underrated tool in any director's bag.

author: IGN YouTube
text:
GTA V's Trevor Was a Big F**k You to Haters
Rockstar's leading men have all reached iconic status, and the best of them are deeply complex: from Niko Bellic’s tragic yearning for a better life, to Arthur Morgan’s solemn journey of redemption. But in GTA V, Rockstar pulled off its most audacious narrative trick with Trevor Philips: a character who completely solves the gap between story and player agency. Trevor isn't just another open-world antihero; he is the literal manifestation of how we play Grand Theft Auto, gleefully reflecting the player's worst instincts.

From his shocking, murderous introduction (RIP Johnny Klebitz) to his surprising moral code, Trevor bridges the gap between sandbox arsonist and writer's voice. Behind the crude violence and satirical absurdity lies Rockstar North at its absolute creative peak, using Trevor to deliver a middle finger to legacy media outrage and moral panic. As we look ahead to Jason and Lucia’s love story in GTA VI, it's worth examining why Trevor Philips remains the ultimate embodiment of Grand Theft Auto's darkest, most human satire.

Join open-world obsessive Jim Trinca as he explores the legacy of Grand Theft Auto 5, Trevor Philips' backstory, the narrative chops of Rockstar North, Ludonarrative Dissonance in video games, Niko Bellic in GTA IV and Arthur Morgan in Red Dead Redemption 2, Steven Ogg's brilliant performance, and the evolution of Grand Theft Auto VI characters Jason and Lucia.

Check out The Trinca Perspective playlist on IGN!
